title: Smile and Winter
premise: Orsen Fairweather hosts the graveyard shift at a dying AM station, taking calls from listeners who died the previous week—calls she alone can hear, and which she has kept secret to protect her fragile found family at the station. When photographs from her late grandmother's house begin showing an extra chair, Orsen realizes the dead aren't just calling in; they're gathering, and they want her to sing the last verse of a lullaby her grandmother taught her—a verse that, once sung, will bind her permanently to their world. Torn between loyalty to the living who love her and the truth that she was always meant to be one of the gathered, Orsen learns the verse but refuses to sing it, instead teaching it back to the dead so they can release themselves. In the end she keeps her life and her voice, but every photograph now shows an empty chair where she used to sit.
about_author: Ines Ravensworth is the pen name of a former late-night radio producer who spent six years answering calls from strangers in the dark before turning to fiction. She writes horror about quiet places—kitchens, studios, empty roads—where the dead are patient and the living are polite.

chapters.title: Dead Air
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. On the graveyard shift, a caller describes his own funeral with cheerful precision; Orsen plays his requested song and logs the call like weather. We meet the station's skeleton crew: engineer Dev, intern Marisol, station manager Ruth. Emotional beat: eerie calm masking loneliness—the show is her only family ritual.

chapters.title: The House That Counts Doors
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. She inherits grandma's house and walks its rooms counting doors aloud, a childhood habit she can't explain. The house feels attentive. A neighbor mentions grandma 'kept the lights on for someone.' Emotional beat: unease braided with grief; the house is a character waiting to speak.

chapters.title: Caller on Line Two
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. More dead callers, each asking for songs and each mentioning 'the chair.' Dev notices Orsen talking into dead air and covers for her without being asked—an act of loyalty that deepens their bond. Emotional beat: warmth against dread; the secret is becoming shared weight.

chapters.title: Photographs
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Helping sort grandma's photos, Marisol spots an extra wooden chair in images from three different decades—in the kitchen, the church, the studio's lobby. She says nothing, but starts photographing everything herself. Emotional beat: protective suspicion; Marisol loves Orsen enough to investigate quietly.

chapters.title: The Lullaby Fragment
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. She finds sheet music in grandma's piano bench: a lullaby with two verses written out and a third marked only 'last verse—do not sing along.' Humming the first two verses makes the house lights flicker in rhythm. Emotional beat: temptation; the song wants to be finished.

chapters.title: Ruth's Rules
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV. Flashback-tinged chapter: Ruth reveals the station once had another overnight host who vanished in 1979, leaving tapes of callers who hadn't called yet. Ruth gives Orsen one rule: never put a dead caller on the air live. Emotional beat: mentorship and warning; the family closes ranks around its newest member.

chapters.title: Winter Settles In
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. An ice storm knocks out power across town, but the studio generator holds, and the calls keep coming—from houses with no phones. Each caller now asks not for songs but for Orsen by name. Emotional beat: isolation sharpening into siege; the dead are closing in politely.

chapters.title: The Extra Chair Arrives
chapters.summary: Dev's POV. Dev delivers a space heater to grandma's house and finds a wooden chair in the kitchen that matches the photographs exactly—old, worn, warm to the touch. He moves it to the curb; it's back inside before he reaches his truck. Emotional beat: terror through a skeptic's eyes; denial collapses.

chapters.title: What Grandma Kept
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. In the attic she finds grandma's journals: decades of entries tracking the chair, the calls, and a family gift—Fairweather women hear the recently dead. Grandma spent her life refusing the last verse, and it cost her everyone she loved. Emotional beat: inheritance as burden; Orsen understands her invisibility was training.

chapters.title: Marisol Asks Questions
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Marisol confronts Orsen gently with the photo evidence. Orsen confesses everything—the calls, the song, the rule. Instead of recoiling, Marisol asks how she can help. Emotional beat: found family tested and confirmed; truth strengthens loyalty rather than breaking it.

chapters.title: The Caller Who Wasn't Dead Yet
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. A caller asks for a song scheduled for tomorrow night—and dies in a crash en route home mid-request. Orsen realizes the show doesn't just receive the dead; it forecasts them. Guilt lands hard: could she have warned him? Emotional beat: crushing responsibility; the gift becomes a debt.

chapters.title: Ruth Breaks Her Own Rule
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV. Ruth admits the vanished 1979 host was her sister, who sang the last verse live on air and was 'gathered.' Ruth has kept the station running ever since as a lighthouse for others like them. Emotional beat: grief finally spoken; the family's history is Orsen's possible future.

chapters.title: Learning the Verse
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. The dead callers begin teaching Orsen the last verse in fragments, each contribution costing them presence—they dim as they give. She transcribes it, refusing to sing. The chair appears in new photographs taken hours ago. Emotional beat: terrible intimacy; the dead are generous, and that's worse.

chapters.title: Counting Doors at 3 A.M.
chapters.summary: Dev's POV. Dev stays the night at grandma's house as backup and witnesses the house counting along with Orsen—doors, windows, chairs. The count ends one higher than it should. Something sits in the extra chair when neither of them looks directly at it. Emotional beat: solidarity under siege; humor fraying into fear.

chapters.title: The Gathering
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Every dead listener calls at once, voices layered into harmony, singing the first two verses through the board. The station's dead air fills with a congregation. Ruth, Dev, and Marisol hold the studio doors—there are more doors than there were. Emotional beat: awe tipping toward apocalypse; the song is almost complete.

chapters.title: Loyalty vs. Truth
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Marisol begs Orsen to burn the transcription and quit the show; Dev argues the dead deserve their song; Ruth says either choice damns someone. Orsen must choose between the family keeping her alive and the truth of what she owes the dead. Emotional beat: the thematic crucible; love pulls both directions.

chapters.title: The Broadcast
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. On air, Orsen announces she will sing the last verse—but instead sings the first two verses back to the dead, then teaches the last verse note by note, making them sing it to each other while she stays silent. The studio fills with light like snowfall. Emotional beat: climax; cleverness and compassion over sacrifice, voice withheld as defiance.

chapters.title: Release
chapters.summary: Dev's POV. One by one the callers say goodbye, each naming a small kindness Orsen gave them on air. The extra chair empties, ages, and crumbles to ash in the kitchen. The house's count finally comes out even. Emotional beat: catharsis; grief transformed into gratitude.

chapters.title: Aftermath
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV. Weeks later, the calls stop. Ruth retires the overnight slot's old tapes, and she and Orsen visit the grave of Ruth's sister, who is finally, verifiably gone. Ruth gives Orsen the 1979 host's microphone. Emotional beat: mourning completed; succession and healing.

chapters.title: The Empty Chair
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Orsen finds that every photograph of her—at the station, with friends, in grandma's albums—now shows an empty chair where she stood, as if she'd already been gathered once and returned. She keeps the photos visible anyway. Emotional beat: bittersweet cost; identity permanently marked by the threshold she refused to cross.

chapters.title: Smile and Winter
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. The crew spends a snowed-in night at the station playing requests from very much living listeners. Orsen hums only the first two verses, smiling. Marisol watches her friend choose, nightly, to stay. Emotional beat: warmth after horror; found family as deliberate daily act.

chapters.title: Sign-Off
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Final broadcast: Orsen signs off with her new ritual—lights on, doors counted, one chair left deliberately empty at the studio 'for whoever needs to sit.' A single call comes in: static, then a child humming two verses. Orsen smiles, and lets the phone ring. Emotional beat: quiet open door; the story ends holding its breath, loyal to both worlds.
